lesson.title: Inside the Envelope: Anatomy of a UDP Datagram
lesson.summary: A UDP datagram is the concrete, self-contained unit UDP uses to carry data, an 8-byte header plus payload that is never linked to any other datagram by the protocol itself.
lesson.body:
A datagram, in general, is a self contained unit of data that carries its own addressing and travels independently, with no relationship enforced between it and any other unit sent before or after it. A UDP datagram is exactly that general idea made concrete at the transport layer: it is the specific envelope UDP uses to hand data to the network, and because UDP is connectionless, the protocol genuinely does not relate one datagram to the next in any way, there is no shared sequence space, no session, no memory of what was sent before.

The header is only 8 bytes, split into four 16 bit fields. The source port identifies the sending process, and it is technically optional, it can be set to zero if no reply is expected. The destination port is required, since it is how the receiving host knows which process should get the data. The length field records the total size of the datagram, header plus payload, in bytes. The checksum, computed over the header, the payload, and a pseudo header borrowed from the IP layer, offers a basic check against accidental corruption in transit, though it is not a security mechanism. Because the length field is 16 bits, and because a UDP datagram travels inside an IP packet, the largest possible UDP payload over IPv4 is 65,507 bytes, which is the maximum 65,535 byte IP packet size minus the 20 byte IP header and the 8 byte UDP header.

A concrete example helps make the header real. Picture a DNS query datagram: source port 51820, an arbitrary ephemeral port chosen by the client, destination port 53, the well known DNS port, and a length field equal to 8 bytes of UDP header plus roughly 29 bytes for a small DNS question, for a total length of about 37 bytes, with the checksum computed over all of it. A datagram that small fits comfortably inside a single IP packet, so a routine DNS query does not need to be fragmented across multiple IP packets to travel.

The independence built into this design has a direct practical consequence: if an application sends three datagrams back to back, the network is free to deliver them out of order, delay one relative to the others, or drop the middle one entirely, and UDP itself will never notice, retry, or reorder anything on the application's behalf. Each datagram really is a standalone envelope from the moment it leaves the sender to the moment, or non moment, it arrives.
